newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy confident France will back NATO command deal.
newsitem.headline: Italy confident France will back NATO command deal.

text.p: Italy said after talks with U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen on Friday that it was confident France could accept a compromise deal to resolve a row over who should command NATO forces in southern Europe.
Foreign Minister Lamberto Dini said a proposal to defer a decision on the command for at least five years had already been accepted by the rest of the alliance.
"We are encouraged by the fact that all other members of NATO would seem to consider this a reasonable approach to the problem," Dini told a joint news conference with Cohen.
"We are confident that also France may find it acceptable."
NATO's southern command, covering the volatile Mediterranean region and based in the Italian port of Naples, is led by an American admiral.

The divisive debate over France's demand that Washington hand over or share the command with Europe had jeopardised an earlier pledge by Paris that its forces would rejoin NATO's military structure after an absence of more than 30 years.
Italian Defence Minister Beniamino Andreatta, who met Cohen separately, said the compromise proposal had emerged from recent talks in Bonn among a number of European NATO countries.

Italy wanted a greater European presence in NATO's command structures but Rome did not believe the time was right to end American leadership in the southern region given Greek-Turkish tensions and general security concerns, Andreatta said.

Cohen said Washington considered it appropriate to defer the command issue for five, six or seven years and then review the question "without any prejudice". He called the recommendation "a very constructive proposal".
"We want very much for France to come in to NATO and we hope, by virtue of seeking constructive ways in which we can help bring that about, that that can become a reality," he said.
Washington had until now refused to surrender the command to a European officer, arguing that a preponderance of southern forces are American including the powerful U.S. Sixth Fleet.

First suggestions that a compromise was being discussed emerged during Cohen's visit to Bonn on Tuesday. France said the following day that it was studying proposals to end the dispute "with a will to reach an agreement".

Cohen, who has also visited Bosnia during his European tour, later flew to Brussels for meetings with NATO Secretary-General Javier Solana and permanent representatives to the alliance before returning to Washington.
His talks in Rome also dealt with NATO plans to expand into eastern Europe, alliance relations with Russia and the situation in the Balkans, including the unrest in Albania.
The alliance campaign for expansion faces a crucial moment at a NATO summit in Madrid in July when the first post-Cold War invitations to ex-communist states are to be issued.
Russian President Boris Yeltsin, in his annual state of the nation address on Thursday, attacked NATO's plans, calling them an attempt to "squeeze" Russia out of Europe.

Cohen said talks on a NATO charter with Russia, designed to allay Moscow's fears, were proceeding positively ahead of President Bill Clinton's March 20-21 summit with Yeltsin. But he stressed that enlargement by the alliance would go ahead.
"We think that (the charter) is important but we also believe that NATO enlargement must go forward and will go forward," Cohen said.
